narrative.theme: Sovereign Developer Verification & The Limits of Generative AI
narrative.tone: Reflective, unvarnished, forensic, and grounded
narrative.topic: The Mirage of Competence: AI Slop & Domain Boundaries

plot_arc.inciting_incident: Recording underneath high-tension power wires resulting in massive electrical hum and an apparent audio-video clock desync, kicking off an adventure into AI forensics and articles on verifiable competence.
plot_arc.rising_action: Prompting frontier models for audio restoration and watching them produce authoritative, hallucinated DSP pipelines and bogus drift ratios, followed by returning to the trail to re-attempt the physical scenario under the conductors.
plot_arc.climax: Constructing deterministic Python DSP notch filters and spectral gating to salvage the audio, verifying whether the filter was a brittle one-off or a reproducible general-purpose tool.
plot_arc.resolution: The cautionary realization that when AI models project fluent competence far beyond our ability to verify, sovereign testing and empirical ground truth are the only real safeguards against catastrophic failure.

narrative.core_inquiry: When AI models project effortless confidence across specialized technical domains, how does an experienced engineer determine where competence ends and plausible falsehood begins?
narrative.chicago_context: Echoes the early Chicago craftsmanship ethos: rejecting vendor marketing claims in favor of empirical, reproducible tests and shared practitioner honesty.
narrative.ai_era_parallel: The defining challenge of Staff+ engineering in 2026: maintaining cognitive control over system boundaries rather than passively accepting synthetic code generation. Grounded in the Watts synthesis: Alan Watts warned IBM engineers in 1969 not to mistake the net of discrete tokens for the living organism, while Peter Watts demonstrated in Blindsight that high-throughput symbol manipulation can simulate intelligence without comprehension.

teleprompter_script.act_1: Welcome to The Sound Above: Minus Zero. I am Mike Hall. In October 2026, I walked out underneath 345,000-volt transmission lines in Northern Illinois with a smartphone to record some thoughts on software craftsmanship and identity. When I checked the footage back at my desk, the audio sounded completely destroyed: deafening 60 Hz electromagnetic hum, corona arcing, and an apparent three-and-a-half-minute clock drift between the audio and video. Trashing the footage and reshooting is the standard advice. But working through that desync kicked off an adventure: a series of articles on the mirage of competence, and a living case study in what happens when we lean on modern AI models. The bottleneck in engineering is never generation: it is verification.
teleprompter_script.act_2: I started with a simple thirteen-word query in a browser, then brought it into Gemini Flash through the terminal. The model immediately leapt into action: generating cascaded Butterworth filter equations, calculating exact duration ratios, and asserting with supreme, effortless confidence that the audio clock had drifted by twenty percent. It gave me shell scripts, math, and complete DSP pipelines. And it was all totally wrong. In Hollywood, investigators yell 'Enhance!' and pixels appear out of thin air. In software, that wishful thinking produces hallucinated AI slop. It reminds me of the Dell Studio XPS laptop I carried during the 2009 Obtiva days, with the sticker that read: 'Typing is not the bottleneck.' In 2026, generating code is not the bottleneck either. The bottleneck is domain understanding.
teleprompter_script.act_3: The container reported 21 minutes of video and only 18 minutes of audio. The model assumed linear drift and handed me atempo=0.837. When I tested the audio in my headphones, it was slurred and completely out of sync. So we went back to ground truth: high-FPS frame extraction, Whisper subtitle alignment, and audio waveforms. What actually happened? At 18 minutes, I said 'Thank you' and wrapped the talk. The remaining three and a half minutes was just me walking with the camera running in silence. The speech was at 1.0x normal speed all along. When AI models project effortless competence, how do you verify where competence ends and plausible falsehood begins? You verify with empirical tests, not conversational trust.
teleprompter_script.act_4: Let us look at the raw recording from the phone. Modern smartphones use dual microphones for noise suppression. The secondary microphone at the top was an unshielded inductive loop antenna, picking up 65 times more electromagnetic rumble from the overhead transmission towers than the bottom microphone. Isolating the bottom microphone gave us clean speech buried under the noise. And I did not leave it there as a single lucky fix. In a recent Ramblin' monologue, I walked right back out under those same high-tension wires. I walked up the rise toward the conductors to deliberately re-attempt the scenario that caused the original disruption. I wanted to see if the interference would hit the phone again, and whether our dehum filter was a brittle one-off or a reproducible general-purpose tool.
teleprompter_script.act_5: That field re-test gets to the heart of our cautionary tale. When you prompt a frontier model outside your domain, it hands you equations and DSP code with total, unblinking fluency. It makes you look like an audio engineering expert. But you are throwing a ball high into the air. If you throw it too high, far beyond your ability to verify and catch it, it comes crashing straight down on your head. Was our filter a permanent engineering asset, or an overfitted artifact of a single chat session? When we ran the re-attempt footage through the same deterministic pipeline, the parameters held. It ran in 40 milliseconds, stripped the hum, and preserved clean voice. But the warning remains: AI models can reach far beyond accessible, verifiable competence. They simulate mastery without comprehension, like the Chinese room in Peter Watts' Blindsight. Our job as engineers is not to marvel at synthetic fluency. Our job is to walk back under the wires, test the boundaries, and machine the output into deterministic code we own.
teleprompter_script.act_6: That is the spirit of The Sound Above. Across this 37-episode series, we are going to rewatch fifteen years of conversations from the Software Craftsmanship movement, from the early Chicago user groups to the AI horizon, examining how developers tackled architecture, testing, and autonomy before commercial platforms took over. Full transcripts, telemetry, and companion code are open at just3ws.com. If you want to help support our independent hosting and archive preservation, check out patreon.com/whoistechcmty. In Episode 1, we dive into the very first room: Sergio Pereira and Chicago Alt.NET. Until next time: keep your feedback loops fast, and verify your code.

teleprompter_script.act_1: Welcome to The Sound Above. I am Mike Hall, and this is Episode 1 of our technical rewatch series. Today we are going back to November 19, 2011, on-site at Software Craftsmanship North America at the Swissotel in downtown Chicago. My very first guest when we launched the UGtastic interview series was Sergio Pereira, the organizer of Chicago Alt.NET. There is a reason I asked Sergio to sit down first. Chicago Alt.NET was not the first user group I ever walked into or attended. It was the first user group where I ever stood up and gave a presentation.
teleprompter_script.act_2: To understand why that room mattered, you have to remember what enterprise .NET felt like in 2007 and 2008. Most corporate shops treated Microsoft's default box products as the law. If a tool or workflow did not ship inside Visual Studio or MSDN, you were told not to touch it. On April 27, 2007, David Laribee published the Alt.NET Manifesto, setting out four core tenets for developers who refused to accept the default corporate box: First: You are the type of developer who uses what works while keeping an eye out for a better way. Second: You reach outside the mainstream to adopt the best of any community: Open Source, Agile, Java, Ruby, and beyond. Third: You are not content with the status quo. Things can always be better expressed, more elegant, simpler, more mutable, and higher quality. Fourth: You know tools are great, but they only take you so far. It is the principles and knowledge that really matter. That October, developers gathered in Austin for the first Alt.NET Open Spaces, which Martin Fowler documented in his Bliki. Sergio Pereira brought that exact spirit to Chicago. On the second Wednesday of every month at 6:30 PM, right when commuters could catch the Metra back to the suburbs, about 25 of us took the elevator up to Redpoint Technologies on the 84th floor of the Sears Tower. On November 12, 2008, I stood up in that room and gave my first presentation on NHaml alongside Adam Tybor presenting on the Spark view engine.
teleprompter_script.act_3: Here is the question that guides our rewatch today: How do working engineers build practical autonomy inside corporate environments without waiting for vendor permission? When ASP.NET MVC was released, it marked one of the biggest strategic turns in Microsoft history. For nearly a decade, Redmond had insisted on WebForms, complex page lifecycles, and viewstate, hiding the raw HTTP protocol behind corporate-approved controls. The release of ASP.NET MVC was the direct victory of the Ruby community. Frameworks like Rails, Sinatra, and Merb had proved to the entire industry that convention over configuration, lightweight routing, and testable controllers were vastly superior for web development. Microsoft's pivot to MVC was a watershed moment: it proved that when developers look outside the approved corporate checklist and insist on better architecture, even the largest software vendor in the world has to adapt. Alt.NET was never about hating .NET. As Sergio says right at the start of this tape, we were developers who liked .NET, used it every day, and wanted to bring continuous improvement, automated testing, NHibernate, StructureMap, and IronRuby into our daily work.
teleprompter_script.act_4: Let us roll the 2011 hallway conversation with Sergio Pereira. Listen to how Sergio describes the charter of the group: not bringing in polished marketing speakers, but encouraging regular team developers to take the talks they gave at lunch with their coworkers and share them with a room of peers who wanted to see a better way to build software.
teleprompter_script.act_5: How does this connect to where we sit in 2026? In 2008, the default vendor trap was drag-and-drop designer wizards that hid coupling and made unit testing impossible. Today, the default vendor trap is black-box cloud AI generation that produces thousands of lines of unverified code while hiding the domain boundaries underneath. The lesson from Chicago Alt.NET is unchanged: tools are instruments, not religions. You do not accept a workflow just because a vendor ships it as the default. You keep your domain models clean, you run your own fast local verification loops, and you judge every tool by whether it holds up under test.
teleprompter_script.act_6: Thank you for joining Episode 1 of The Sound Above. You can read the full interactive transcript with Sergio Pereira, along with links to David Laribee's 2007 Manifesto, Martin Fowler's Austin notes, Scott Guthrie's early MVC previews, and Jeremy Miller's retrospectives, right on the Episode 1 page at just3ws.com. To help support our independent compute and archive preservation, visit patreon.com/whoistechcmty. In Episode 2, we sit down with Ray Hightower of ChicagoRuby to talk about grassroots hospitality and opening doors across communities. Until next time: keep your feedback loops fast, and your code humane.

teleprompter_script.act_1: Welcome back to The Sound Above. I am Mike Hall, and this is Episode 2. Today we return to SCNA 2011 at the Swissotel in Chicago for my conversation with Ray Hightower, the founder of WisdomGroup and organizer of ChicagoRuby and WindyCityRails. If Sergio Pereira gave me my first user group room in the Sears Tower, Ray Hightower was the ambassador who opened the door to the entire Chicago Ruby and software craftsmanship community.
teleprompter_script.act_2: In late 2008, I was working remotely as Principal Developer at Business Decisions, Inc., maintaining a multi-tenant HR platform and coordinating with developers in Uruguay. I reached out to Ray, and we met up halfway at Midway Restaurant. I was still a Microsoft .NET developer at the time. Ray did not gatekeep or lecture me about platforms. teleprompter_script.act_1: Welcome to The Sound Above: Minus One. I am Mike Hall. On the aluminum lid of the MacBook Air sitting on my desk right now, directly beside the Apple logo, is a circular Dead Rabbit Radio sticker. Most people who see it assume it is ordinary podcast merch. To me, it is a permanent physical artifact of one of the most intense, ambitious, and humbling technical experiments I ever ran. It is the story of how five Raspberry Pis, over one thousand daily podcast episodes, early ChatGPT pairing, and an independent creator named Jason Carpenter taught me how to transcribe audio at scale. And it is the story of how imposter syndrome and cognitive overload caused me to freeze up and walk away, and why those painful lessons directly enabled the automated pipeline running on this machine today.
teleprompter_script.act_2: To understand why this experiment happened, you have to go back to 2013. For four years, I hauled thirty-five pounds of camera gear through conference hallways across the country, recording more than two hundred technical interviews for UGtastic. When the recording finished, I hit an impassable wall: transcription. In 2013, human transcription services cost one to two dollars per minute. For a catalog of two hundred conversations, transcription was a four-figure impossibility for an unfunded grassroots project. Early cloud speech APIs produced phonetic gibberish on words like NHibernate, StructureMap, and NUnit. For nearly ten years, those tapes sat dormant on hard drives. The knowledge was trapped in digital amber.
teleprompter_script.act_3: In late 2022 and early 2023, the world shifted. OpenAI open-sourced Whisper, and Georgi Gerganov released whisper.cpp. Suddenly, the marginal cost of transcription dropped to zero. You did not need a corporate cloud budget. You just needed electricity and CPU cycles. At the time, modern agentic coding tools did not exist. ChatGPT had just introduced GPT-4. I wanted to see if an engineer pairing with an LLM in a browser window could architect a distributed media pipeline from scratch. But I needed a massive dataset. I did not want to risk the precious UGtastic tapes on unverified tools. I needed a single, consistent speaker with hundreds of hours of contiguous audio. That is how I found Dead Rabbit Radio.
teleprompter_script.act_4: Dead Rabbit Radio is a daily podcast hosted, researched, and produced entirely by Jason Carpenter, covering paranormal folklore, conspiracy theories, and historical oddities. Jason is the sole host. There was zero crosstalk, no volume jumps between mics, and Jason spoke with a rhythmic cadence and pacing remarkably similar to my own speaking voice. I had five Raspberry Pi single-board computers in my home lab: node01 through node05. I wrote bin/distribution in Ruby to bin-pack audio files across the nodes by total byte size. I wrote bin/distribute to deploy files via Net::SSH and rsync. And on each Pi, bin/transcribe ran whisper.cpp with a mandatory 120-second thermal cooldown between episodes so the quad-core ARM chips did not melt.
teleprompter_script.act_5: Over several weeks, the cluster hummed quietly in my basement. It chewed through the catalog, generating 2,034 distinct transcript files: text files and subtitle tracks for over one thousand episodes. I reached out to Jason Carpenter to ask his blessing, and he was exceptionally gracious, kind, and supportive. But then I hit the cliff. I tried to generalize the tool into a universal podcast aggregator. Immediately, broken RSS feeds, corrupted ID3 tags, and erratic audio formats wrecked my assumptions. At the exact same time, high-severity production incidents and intense Observability architecture at my day job overwhelmed my working memory. I told myself I was an imposter playing with toy scripts. I felt so embarrassed about being unable to sustain the pace that I froze. I stopped updating the repo. I ghosted Jason out of sheer shame, and for months I could not even bring myself to listen to the show.
teleprompter_script.act_6: For a long time, I carried fluffle as a private regret. But craftsmanship teaches us to inspect our scars honestly. That experiment was not a failure; it was the essential skunkworks laboratory that made today possible. It taught me that raw audio must be normalized deterministically before running AI inference. It taught me the Maildir queue architecture that prevents file corruption. It taught me lexical priming to repair proper nouns. And it proved that local hardware sovereignty works. Today, five Raspberry Pis taking two hours per episode have been replaced by Apple Silicon running ztranscribe in ninety seconds. All 218 UGtastic interviews are transcribed and searchable. To Jason Carpenter: thank you for your stories, your generosity, and your craft. The sticker remains on this laptop, and the lessons live in every line of code this system runs today.
